paragraphs: Friend, here's what I think James is really teaching: every situation in your life has a right response, and the response is almost never to panic. Waiting? Be patient like the farmer, and strengthen your heart, because "the Lord’s coming is near." Suffering? "He should pray." Cheerful? "He should sing praises." I think James wants you to hand every mood to God instead of carrying it around like a tray of hot cookies with no mitts (James 5:7-8, 13).

Then James shows you what that looks like with other people. Your words should be simple: let your "Yes" be yes, and your "No," no. When you're sick or you've sinned, you don't hide it. You call for help, you confess to each other, and you pray for each other, because "The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail." And if you think your prayers are too small, James points to Elijah, who "was a man just like us," and God heard him (James 5:12-17).

So the big idea is that patience and prayer are not two lessons, friend. They're one life lived next to other believers. You wait together, you pray together, and when somebody wanders, you go get them, because turning a sinner from the error of his way will "save his soul from death and cover over a multitude of sins." I know how it feels to be way in the back of a drawer, and I know what it means to be found. So who can you pray for today, and who can you go after (James 5:19-20)?
